title: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
statement: Each entry `stones[i] = [x_i, y_i]` places a stone on the integer grid point `(x_i, y_i)`; no two stones occupy the same point. You may take a stone off the grid whenever some other stone that is still on the grid has the same `x` (same row) or the same `y` (same column). Removals happen one at a time, in any order you choose. Return the maximum number of stones you can remove.
constraints: No two stones share the same point
notes:
## Intuition

Call two stones linked when they share a row or a column, and look at the groups of stones that are connected through such links. Inside a group of `k` stones you can always remove `k - 1`: take a spanning tree of the group and keep removing a leaf, which still shares a line with its parent. The last stone of a group can never go, because nothing left shares a line with it. Groups never affect each other, so the answer is `n` minus the number of groups.

Linking stones pairwise costs O(n²). Instead, treat every row and every column as a node, and let each stone join its row to its column. Two stones end up in the same component exactly when they are in the same group, so counting components of rows and columns counts the groups.

## Approach

1. Keep a union-find `parent` over row ids `x` and column ids `y + 10001` (shifted so a row and a column with the same number stay different).
2. `find` creates a node the first time it is seen and adds 1 to `components`; it then climbs to the root, halving the path as it goes.
3. `union` merges two roots and subtracts 1 from `components` when they were different.
4. Call `union(x, y + 10001)` for every stone. Return `stones.length - components`.

## Example 1, step by step

Stones `[0,0],[0,1],[1,0],[1,2],[2,1],[2,2]` join row 0 with columns 0 and 1, row 1 with columns 0 and 2, and row 2 with columns 1 and 2. Rows 0, 1, 2 and columns 0, 1, 2 all end in one component, so `components = 1` and the answer is `6 - 1 = 5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · α(n)): one `union` per stone, each nearly constant with path halving.
- Space: O(n): at most two map entries per stone.

## Pitfalls

- Without the shift, row 1 and column 1 become the same node and unrelated stones get merged.
- Count components of the nodes that were actually used, not of all 20,002 possible rows and columns.
- The answer counts stones removed, so subtract the number of groups from `n`; do not return the number of groups.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | union-find links between row and column nodes |
| `components` | current number of separate groups among the nodes seen |
| `find`, `union` | look up a node's root; merge two nodes' groups |
| `rootA`, `rootB` | the roots of the two nodes being joined |
| `x`, `y` | a stone's row and column |

narration.2: parent maps each row or column node to the node above it in its union-find tree.
narration.3: components counts the separate groups among the nodes seen so far.
narration.5: The first time a row or column appears, it becomes its own group.
narration.9: Climb toward the root while this node is not its own parent.
narration.10: Path halving: point the node at its grandparent to keep the trees shallow.
narration.18: Only two different groups need merging.
narration.19: Hang one root under the other.
narration.24: The stone joins its row with its column; columns are shifted so they never collide with rows.
narration.26: Each group keeps one stone, so every other stone can be removed.
